interactions.label: A 3-month-old formula-fed infant presents with frequent effortless regurgitation

params.question: A 3-month-old formula-fed infant presents with frequent effortless regurgitation after feeds but is gaining weight normally along the 50th centile. What is the most appropriate first-line management?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Proton pump inhibitors are reserved for GORD with complications such as oesophagitis, faltering growth, or Sandifer syndrome. This infant is thriving on the 50th centile, so conservative measures are the appropriate first line.

answers.text: Thicken feeds, position upright after feeds, and offer smaller, more frequent feeds

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Physiological GOR in a thriving infant is managed conservatively: thicken feeds with rice-based thickening agents, upright positioning for 20–30 minutes after feeds, and smaller, more frequent feeds. These measures suffice for the majority of cases.

answers.text: Order an upper GI contrast study to exclude malrotation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This infant has effortless regurgitation with normal growth — a classic physiological GOR presentation. Upper GI imaging is reserved when red flag features are present, such as bilious or projectile vomiting, dysphagia, or growth faltering.

Surgical fundoplication is the last resort, reserved for severe refractory GORD that has failed both conservative and pharmacological management. It is not appropriate for an infant with uncomplicated physiological GOR.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle is matching management intensity to disease severity. A thriving infant with effortless regurgitation has physiological GOR — conservative measures (thicken feeds, upright positioning for 20–30 minutes, smaller frequent feeds) are first-line and sufficient for most cases.

Well done. Physiological GOR in a thriving infant responds to simple conservative measures — feed thickening, upright positioning, and smaller frequent feeds. Pharmacotherapy is reserved for complicated GORD with documented complications.

interactions.label: A 2-year-old child is brought to the emergency department after crying vigorousl

params.question: A 2-year-old child is brought to the emergency department after crying vigorously following a fall, stopping breathing, turning blue, becoming limp, and recovering spontaneously within one minute. What is the most accurate statement regarding diagnosis?

answers.text: An EEG is mandatory to exclude epilepsy before diagnosing a breath-holding spell

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: BHS is not epilepsy, and an EEG is not required when the history is typical. The presence of a clear emotional trigger followed by vigorous crying before the spell distinguishes it from epilepsy, where seizures occur without this antecedent sequence.

answers.text: A normal echocardiogram must be obtained before confirming the diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Echocardiography is not part of the routine BHS evaluation. Cardiac investigations are reserved only when the history suggests a cardiac arrhythmia — for instance, spells triggered by exercise or occurring without an emotional trigger.

answers.text: The diagnosis is clinical, based on the sequence: trigger → cry → colour change → spell → recovery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Breath-holding spells are diagnosed from a structured history eliciting the characteristic sequence: emotional trigger → vigorous cry → apnoea with colour change → transient limpness or loss of consciousness → spontaneous recovery. No investigation is needed when this sequence is clearly present.

answers.text: Breath-holding spells cannot be diagnosed until all organic causes have been excluded by investigation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: BHS is a positive clinical diagnosis made from a typical history, not a diagnosis of exclusion. The paediatrician should complete a structured history before considering investigations, as the diagnosis is almost always apparent from the history alone.

overallFeedback.feedback: Breath-holding spells are a clinical diagnosis. The key is eliciting the characteristic sequence from the history: emotional trigger → vigorous cry → apnoea with colour change → spell → spontaneous recovery. Investigations are reserved for atypical presentations only.
Exactly right. A structured history revealing the trigger → cry → colour change → spell → recovery sequence clinches the diagnosis. Resist the impulse to investigate before completing the history.

interactions.label: A mother describes her 2-year-old holding his breath briefly during tantrums. Wh

params.question: A mother describes her 2-year-old holding his breath briefly during tantrums. Which clinical feature most reliably distinguishes a temper tantrum with breath-holding from a breath-holding spell?

answers.text: Absence of colour change (cyanosis or pallor) and absence of loss of consciousness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Tantrums may include brief breath-holding, but crucially this does not progress to cyanosis, pallor, or loss of consciousness. In true breath-holding spells, involuntary apnoea leads to visible colour change and, in severe cases, transient LOC — this is the key clinical distinction.

answers.text: The episode being triggered by frustration or a denied request

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both temper tantrums and cyanotic breath-holding spells are triggered by emotional upset such as frustration or denied requests. The trigger alone does not distinguish between the two conditions.

answers.text: The child falling to the floor during the episode

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Falling to the floor is common in tantrums but can also occur in BHS when the child loses consciousness. This motor behaviour does not reliably differentiate the two conditions.

answers.text: The episode lasting longer than five minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Episode duration varies widely in tantrums and is typically brief in BHS, but duration alone is not the defining distinction. The presence or absence of colour change and loss of consciousness is the discriminating feature.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinguishing feature is the presence or absence of colour change and loss of consciousness. In temper tantrums, breath-holding does NOT cause cyanosis, pallor, or LOC. In breath-holding spells, involuntary apnoea leads to visible colour change and may cause transient loss of consciousness.

Correct. The critical distinction is the absence of colour change and loss of consciousness. Tantrums may include breath-holding, but it does not progress to cyanosis, pallor, or LOC as it does in true breath-holding spells.

interactions.label: A 6-year-old boy who has never achieved consistent nighttime dryness wets the be

params.question: A 6-year-old boy who has never achieved consistent nighttime dryness wets the bed four to five nights per week. Physical examination and urine dipstick are normal. What is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

answers.text: Order renal ultrasound to exclude structural anomalies

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Renal ultrasound is not indicated routinely in primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis. It is reserved for specific indications such as suspected structural anomalies, recurrent urinary tract infections, or features suggesting non-MNE.

answers.text: Refer for urodynamic studies to assess detrusor function

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Urodynamic studies are invasive and reserved for specific indications such as suspected detrusor overactivity with daytime symptoms or non-MNE that has not responded to initial management. They are not part of the routine work-up for primary MNE.

Although desmopressin is effective for nocturnal polyuria-driven enuresis, treatment should follow proper classification. A bladder diary identifies whether nocturnal polyuria is the dominant mechanism, guiding the choice between desmopressin and alarm therapy.

answers.text: Maintain a bladder diary to quantify urine volumes and identify nocturnal polyuria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In primary MNE with a normal examination and dipstick, the bladder diary is the key next step. It quantifies nocturnal urine production and functional bladder capacity, classifying the enuresis subtype and guiding the choice of management — desmopressin for polyuria, alarm for reduced bladder capacity.

overallFeedback.feedback: For primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis with a normal examination and dipstick, the next step is a bladder diary to quantify urine volumes and identify nocturnal polyuria. Resist ordering renal ultrasound or urodynamic studies routinely — these are reserved for specific clinical indications identified through systematic assessment.

Well done. In primary MNE with a normal examination, the bladder diary adds clinical precision by quantifying nocturnal urine volumes and functional bladder capacity — this guides appropriate management without unnecessary invasive investigations.
